skills.name: Factorise cubic polynomials using the factor theorem

note.text:
To factorise a cubic f(x):
1. Find one root k by trial: try the factors of the number term (±1, ±2, …) until f(k) = 0.
2. Then (x − k) is a factor. Divide f(x) by (x − k) to get a quadratic.
3. Factorise the quadratic.
Example: x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6. f(1) = 0, so (x − 1) is a factor; x³ − 2x² − 5x + 6 = (x − 1)(x² − x − 6) = (x − 1)(x − 3)(x + 2).
Check by expanding, or by checking that f(3) = 0 and f(−2) = 0.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text:
By the end, you should be able to factorise a cubic completely by finding one root with the factor theorem, dividing, and factorising the quadratic.
Builds on: Lesson {13} (factor theorem), Lesson {12} (division) and Lesson {5} (trinomials).
Leads to: Lesson {15} (solving cubic equations) and sketching cubic graphs.

sections.heading: Finding the first factor
sections.text:
A cubic such as f(x) = {cubic(1, -2, -5, 6)} has no common factor and no grouping. Use the factor theorem.
If (x − k) is a factor with whole numbers, then k divides the number term {6}. So try {1}, {-1}, {2}, {-2}, {3}, {-3}, …
• f({1}) = {1} − {2} − {5} + {6} = {0}. Found: (x − {1}) is a factor.
Stop at the first value that gives {0}.

sections.heading: Dividing and finishing
sections.text:
Divide f(x) by (x − {1}) (long division or by matching terms): {cubic(1, -2, -5, 6)} = (x − {1})({quad(1, -1, -6)}).
Now factorise the quadratic as in Lesson {5}: {quad(1, -1, -6)} = {lin2(1, -3, 1, 2)}.
So f(x) = (x − {1})(x − {3})(x + {2}).
Check with the factor theorem: f({3}) = {27} − {18} − {15} + {6} = {0} and f({-2}) = {-8} − {8} + {10} + {6} = {0}.

key_words.meaning: a polynomial of degree {3}, such as {cubic(1, -2, -5, 6)}
trying values one by one until one works
go on until every factor is linear or cannot be split

mistake.why: x − {2} is zero when x = {2}. The factor has the opposite sign to the root.

worked_example.problem: Factorise f(x) = {cubic(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r)}.
steps: Try factors of {-p * q * r}: f({p}) = {cval(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r, p)}, so (x − {p}) is a factor.
Divide by (x − {p}): the quotient is {quad(1, -(q + r), q * r)}.
Factorise the quadratic: {quad(1, -(q + r), q * r)} = {lin2(1, -q, 1, -r)}.
checks: cval(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r, p) == 0

cards.idea: Try the factors of the number term until f(k) = {0}: that gives a first factor (x − k).
Divide by (x − k) to reduce the cubic to a quadratic.

check.prompt: Factorise completely {cubic(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r)}.

misconceptions.explain: A root k gives the factor (x − k): the signs in the brackets are opposite to the roots.
'Completely': the quadratic {quad(1, -(q + r), q * r)} still factorises.
Expand the last two brackets: their product has the wrong middle sign.

solution: f({p}) = {0}, so ({poly([1, 'x'], [-p, ''])}) is a factor; dividing gives {quad(1, -(q + r), q * r)}.

questions.prompt: f(x) = {cubic(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r)}. Which of these makes f(x) = {0}?
solution: f({p}) = {cval(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r, p)}.

questions.prompt: ({poly([1, 'x'], [-p, ''])}) is a factor of {cubic(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r)}. Then the cubic = ({poly([1, 'x'], [-p, ''])})(x² + Bx + C). Find C.

misconceptions.explain: C times {br(-p)} gives {-p * q * r}: divide by {br(-p)}.
{br(-p)} × C = {-p * q * r}, so C = {q * r}. Check the signs.

solution: Compare number terms: {br(-p)} × C = {-p * q * r}.

questions.prompt: Factorise {cubic(1, -(p + q + r), p * q + p * r + q * r, -p * q * r)} and give the largest value of x that makes it zero.

misconceptions.explain: (x − k) is zero when x = k: the signs of the roots are opposite to the numbers in the brackets.

solution: Find a root by trial, divide, and factorise the quadratic: ({poly([1, 'x'], [-p, ''])})({poly([1, 'x'], [-q, ''])})({poly([1, 'x'], [-r, ''])}).
The values that make it zero are {p}, {q} and {r}.

questions.prompt: Factorise completely {cubic(2, -(1 + 2 * (q + r)), q + r + 2 * q * r, -q * r)}.

misconceptions.explain: Check x = {2}: f({2}) = {cval(2, -(1 + 2 * (q + r)), q + r + 2 * q * r, -q * r, 2)}, not {0}. The root is {frac(1, 2)}.
({poly([2, 'x'], [1, ''])}) is zero at x = {frac(-1, 2)}, but f({frac(-1, 2)}) is not {0}.

solution: Try factors: f({q}) = {0}, so ({poly([1, 'x'], [-q, ''])}) is a factor; f({r}) = {0} too.
Dividing by both leaves a linear factor with {mono(2, 'x')}: f({frac(1, 2)}) = {0}, so ({poly([2, 'x'], [-1, ''])}) is a factor.
